holidays.name: Fibonacci Day
holidays.description: Math lovers celebrate the date written as 11/23, which gives the digits 1, 1, 2, 3. Those are the first numbers of the famous Fibonacci sequence, where each number is the sum of the two before it. Fans mark the day with spiral-shaped snacks, pinecone hunts, and sunflower spotting.
holidays.origin: It is an unofficial observance created by math fans. The date works because 1, 1, 2, 3 are the opening numbers of the sequence. It is named for Leonardo of Pisa, known as Fibonacci, who popularized the sequence in Europe in 1202.
holidays.funFact: Fibonacci did not invent the sequence. Indian mathematicians had described it centuries earlier, and he introduced it to Europe in his book Liber Abaci while using it to model rabbit population growth.

holidays.name: National Espresso Day
holidays.description: A day to honor the small, intense shot of coffee that fuels mornings, meetings, and tiramisu. Celebrate with a double shot, a cortado, or an espresso-poured affogato for dessert.
holidays.origin: This is an unofficial observance of unclear origin, popular with coffee lovers and cafés. The drink itself began in Italy in the early 1900s, when machines were built to brew coffee fast under pressure.
holidays.funFact: A single shot of espresso usually has less caffeine than a full cup of drip coffee. The strong flavor comes from concentration, not from a bigger caffeine dose.

holidays.name: National Cashew Day
holidays.description: A day for crunching on one of the creamiest nuts around. Eat them roasted, blend them into vegan cheese, or stir them into a curry.
holidays.origin: This is an unofficial observance of unclear origin, popular with snack lovers and nut fans.
holidays.funFact: The cashew is a seed that hangs from the bottom of a fruit called the cashew apple. Raw cashew shells contain a skin-irritating oil related to the one in poison ivy, so cashews are always processed before they reach store shelves.
